subject: chemistry
title: Practical: temperature changes in reactions
key_idea: To classify a reaction, react known amounts in an insulated cup and measure the temperature before and after. A rise shows an exothermic reaction and a fall shows an endothermic one. Fair tests and repeats make the result reliable.

blocks.text: This practical measures the temperature change when substances react or dissolve in water.

diagram.alt: The steps for measuring a temperature change in a reaction, in order.
diagram.prompt: Put the steps of the method in the correct order.
steps: Measure a known volume of liquid into a polystyrene cup.
Measure the starting temperature with a thermometer.
Add the solid or second solution and stir.
Put a lid on the cup.
Record the highest or lowest temperature reached.

items: Use a **polystyrene cup**. It is a better insulator than glass, so less energy is transferred to the surroundings.
Stir the mixture so the temperature is the same throughout.
Leave the thermometer in the mixture to read the final temperature.
For a solid that dissolves, record the lowest or highest temperature after it has dissolved.

blocks.text: Several types of change in solution can be tested. In each, the temperature change shows the heat change.

rows: Dilute sulfuric acid with potassium hydroxide solution
Magnesium powder with copper sulfate solution
Citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution

blocks.text: Precipitation reactions can be tested in the same way.

items: Measure the start and final temperatures in an insulated cup, with a lid, and stir.
Temperature change = final temperature − initial temperature.

blocks.text: This section covers the variables to control and how to improve accuracy.

items.meaning: The variable you change, such as the mass of solid added.
The variable you measure, such as the temperature change or the highest temperature reached.
A variable kept the same so the test is fair.

items: Keep the same volume of liquid each time.
Keep the same starting temperature and the same concentration of any acid or solution.
To improve accuracy: use a polystyrene cup or insulate the beaker, add a lid, stir, and use a digital or more accurate thermometer.
Use a more accurate balance, and a measuring cylinder or pipette for volumes.
Repeat the experiment and calculate the mean, ignoring anomalous results.

blocks.text: An anomalous result does not fit the pattern. Leave it out when you work out the mean.

blocks.label: Mean temperature change
blocks.formula: mean = sum of the results ÷ number of results
where: results are the temperature changes, in °C

items.text: Results are 9.1, 9.3, 12.0 and 9.2 °C. The 12.0 °C result is much higher than the others.

items: A result such as 16.5 ± 0.3 °C shows the uncertainty. The values lie up to 0.3 °C either side of the mean.
In a reaction that has finished, the temperature of the mixture falls back towards room temperature, because energy is lost to the surroundings.
When acid is added to alkali, the temperature rises until the reaction is complete. It then falls as more acid is added.
Control the volume, starting temperature and concentration so the test is fair.
Insulate, add a lid, stir and repeat to improve accuracy.

checks.q: Why is a polystyrene cup better than a glass beaker for this practical?
checks.a: Polystyrene is a better insulator, so it reduces energy transfer to the surroundings.

checks.q: The temperature changes in three repeats are 8.0, 8.4 and 8.2 °C. Calculate the mean.
Give two variables to keep the same when comparing the temperature change for different masses of a solid.
checks.a: The volume of liquid and the starting temperature of the liquid.

worked_example.question:
This question is about salts. Ammonium nitrate solution is produced when ammonia gas reacts with nitric acid.

Describe a method to investigate how the temperature changes when different masses of ammonium nitrate are dissolved in water.

You do not need to write about safety precautions.
answer_points: Use a suitable container, such as a test tube, with insulation.
Add a measured volume of water.
Measure the initial temperature of the water with a thermometer.
Add a stated mass of ammonium nitrate, for example 1 g, and stir to dissolve it.
Measure the final (lowest) temperature of the solution.
Calculate the temperature difference, or determine it graphically.
Repeat with different masses, using the same volume of water each time.
worked_example.tip: This is a levels question. For the top level, show how the temperature change is found for different masses in the same quantity of water.

worked_example.question:
In an experiment, a solid is mixed with a liquid.

The temperature change of the mixture is measured.

temperature of liquid at start = 18.6 °C
temperature of products at end = 16.1 °C

Calculate the change in temperature.

Give a sign and a unit in your answer.
answer_points: Change = final temperature − initial temperature = 16.1 − 18.6.
The unit is °C, so the answer is −2.5 °C.
worked_example.tip: The answer −2.5 °C scores all three marks even without working. Without the sign it scores 2, and without the sign and unit it scores 1.

worked_example.question:
A group of students are investigating chemical reactions.

They add magnesium powder to copper sulfate solution.

They predict this will cause an increase in temperature, as they believe the reaction is exothermic.

The students collect the apparatus needed to test their theory.

Describe an experiment the students can do to measure the increase in temperature.

You can include a labelled diagram in your answer.
answer_points: Any four from:
Pour a measured volume of copper sulfate solution into an insulated cup.
Measure and record the start temperature.
Add the magnesium powder and stir.
Put on a lid.
Measure and record the maximum (final) temperature.
Repeat the experiment, for example three times.
Calculate the temperature change.
worked_example.tip: One mark for each step. Labelled diagrams can also score.

worked_example.question:
A student investigates the temperature change when solid hydrated sodium carbonate reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid.

She pours 25.0 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid into a polystyrene cup, records the temperature, adds the solid and records the lowest temperature of the mixture.

Explain why it is better to use a polystyrene cup instead of a glass beaker in this experiment.
answer_points: Polystyrene is an insulator.
This reduces the energy transferred from the surroundings to the mixture.
So the temperature decrease is closer to the true value (the results are more accurate).
worked_example.tip: Any two points score. Link the insulator to what it does to the energy transfer.

blocks.text: Combustion can be tested too. A burning fuel heats a known volume of water in a metal container.

items: Measure the temperature rise of the water.
Weigh the fuel burner before and after to find the mass of fuel burned.

blocks.text: The heat energy change can be calculated from the temperature change.

blocks.label: Heat energy change
where: Q is the heat energy change in J
m is the mass of water in g
c is the specific heat capacity of water, 4.2 J/g °C
ΔT is the temperature change in °C

items.text: 25 cm³ of water has a mass of 25 g.
The temperature rises by 7.0 °C, so Q = 25 × 4.2 × 7.0.
